questions.question: What is the planner's responsibility in a plan-execute agent?
options: To produce an ordered list of typed steps the executor will run
To call the dispatcher directly on each step as soon as the step is produced
To enforce per-step and per-session timeouts before any step reaches the executor
To handle the JSON-RPC transport that carries steps between planner and executor
questions.explanation: Planner emits structured plans. The executor runs them, enforces timeouts, and owns the transport. Mixing the two is the chain-of-thought trap this lesson is moving away from.

questions.question: Why is expected_outcome part of the Step shape even though the executor does not check it?
options: Because the dispatcher uses the expected_outcome string as a cache key for idempotency
Because the tool registry requires every registered step to declare an expected outcome
Because the underlying model is fine-tuned on expected_outcome text during training
Because it gives the replanner and tracers a stated success condition to read
questions.explanation: The replanner reads it when revising. The tracer renders it on the timeline. It is a human-readable contract on the step, not a cache key or registry requirement.

questions.question: When a step fails and the replanner returns a new plan, what does the executor emit on the event stream?
options: Nothing is emitted — a replan is applied silently without any event on the stream
plan.diff, listing which step ids were removed, added, and revised in the new plan
session.complete with status=failed, ending the session instead of continuing
tool.error followed immediately by a fresh session.start for the revised plan
questions.explanation: plan.diff makes the revision visible. A silent rewrite is the bug we are avoiding, and the session does not end or restart on a replan.

questions.question: Why have both max_steps and max_replans as separate budgets?
options: Because the asyncio event loop needs two separate counters to schedule tasks correctly
Because the dispatcher rejects any plan that does not declare both budgets up front
Because they measure different units — steps cap total execution, replans cap planner calls
Because the tool registry keeps its own separate count of how many times each tool was replanned
questions.explanation: max_replans catches a planner that keeps returning the same broken plan. max_steps catches a runaway plan that keeps growing.

questions.question: Which reason is returned when the planner returns an empty list on the first call?
options: no_plan — the planner returned zero steps on the very first call
step_budget — the plan grew past the maximum allowed number of total steps
replan_budget — the planner was called more times than allowed
goal_met — the executor decided the goal was already satisfied before any step ran
questions.explanation: No plan, no execution. The session ends with reason=no_plan and status=failed.

questions.question: What is in PlanDiff.revised?
options: Step ids whose tool_name or args changed between the old and new plan revisions
Step ids that were present in the old plan but are absent from the new plan
Step ids that appear in the new plan but did not exist anywhere in the old plan
Step ids the planner marked to be skipped without removing them from the plan
questions.explanation: revised is the set of ids whose (tool_name, args) signature changed across the revision — not the added, removed, or skipped sets.
